interest: This collection provides a fascinating window into the murky intersection of Axis intelligence, multinational trade, and refugee diplomacy during the transition from World War II to the early Cold War. It uniquely documents how Japanese intelligence maintained an active espionage apparatus in Bucharest even after Romania shifted to the Allies and came under Soviet occupation, including an abortive American effort to seize ten tons of Japanese archives before they were burned. Additionally, the extensive interrogations and correspondence regarding Ion Constantinescu provide granular insight into how the Mitsui zaibatsu operated in southeastern Europe, how Romanian procurement agents attempted to secure military supplies in neutral Switzerland and Sweden, and how former Axis figures navigated emerging Cold War tensions and NKVD surveillance in Bern. The file also illustrates the global reach of SCAP's financial blockades on occupied Japan, showing how Allied asset freezes in Tokyo directly affected commercial disputes across Europe.
overview: This file, categorized under State Department decimal classification 894.20271 (Military Activities of Japan in Romania), compiles military intelligence reports, diplomatic airgrams, and official despatches between 1945 and 1947 concerning Japanese espionage networks and wartime commercial intermediaries connected to Romania. It opens with a War Department intelligence report detailing Japanese intelligence operations and document destruction in Bucharest following Romania's armistice, focusing on former military attaché Lieutenant Colonel Tsuneyuki Shimamuki's agent network. The predominant core of the dossier investigates Ion Constantinescu, a Romanian businessman and former Mitsui trust representative who served as an honorary commercial attaché in Tokyo before undertaking wartime procurement missions for the Antonescu regime in Switzerland. Across several diplomatic exchanges between Washington, Bern, Bucharest, and Stockholm, American officials evaluate Constantinescu's denials of Axis espionage, his complex counter-allegations exposing rival Romanian factions and Soviet NKVD operatives in Switzerland, and his persistent, unsuccessful petition to release 312,800 Swiss francs frozen in Tokyo's Yokohama Specie Bank under SCAP occupation controls as he attempted to transit the United States for China. An unrelated concluding telegram details the wartime propaganda activities of Siamese broadcaster Yoa Suthinun in Tokyo.

subfiles.about: A War Department intelligence report detailing Japanese espionage activities, legation funding, and document burning in Bucharest following the severance of diplomatic relations.
subfiles.from: War Department, Military Intelligence Division (initialed EUK)
subfiles.summary: The War Department Military Intelligence Division reports that Japanese personnel in Bucharest maintained substantial freedom of movement despite the formal rupture in relations between Japan and Romania. Before their planned repatriation via air instead of the Trans-Siberian Railroad, the Japanese burned ten tons of documents stored in a warehouse to thwart an American seizure operation. Former military attaché Lieutenant Colonel Tsuneyuki Shimamuki remains active running an espionage network of former German agents targeting Allied missions and arriving U.S. personnel, with legation expenses rising to nearly two million JPI per week.
subfiles.title: War Department Intelligence Report on Japanese Activities in Rumania
subfiles.to: Department of State and Office of Strategic Services

subfiles.about: An instruction directing the Legation in Stockholm to investigate reports concerning Ion Constantinescu's ties to Japanese intelligence and his contacts in Sweden.
subfiles.from: Department of State (signed Dean Acheson, Acting Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: The State Department transmits an intelligence report alleging that Romanian national Ion Constantinescu, a European representative of the Mitsui trusts, joined the Japanese intelligence service while living in Japan from 1936 to 1941. Constantinescu reportedly fled Bucharest for Zurich in August 1944 carrying gold and currency for Mihai Antonescu and was suspected of attempting to travel to Japan via Stockholm. Acting Secretary of State Dean Acheson instructs the Stockholm Legation to verify Constantinescu's whereabouts and investigate his ties with Romanian Legation officials Miron Giroiu and Paul Lahovary.
subfiles.title: State Department Airgram A-74 to Amlegation Stockholm on Ion Constantinescu

subfiles.about: A circular instruction requesting biographical data from the U.S. Mission in Bucharest regarding suspected Japanese intelligence operative Ion Constantinescu and his associates.
subfiles.from: Department of State (signed Dean Acheson, Acting Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: The Department of State sends an airgram to the U.S. Representative in Bucharest repeating the intelligence report regarding Ion Constantinescu's association with Mitsui and Japanese intelligence. The report highlights Constantinescu's flight from Romania to Switzerland with engineer Eugene Botta and government funds, as well as his efforts to reach Stockholm. Acting Secretary Dean Acheson requests that the mission compile and transmit all available biographical information on Constantinescu and the named associates.
subfiles.title: State Department Airgram A-34 to Amrep Bucharest on Ion Constantinescu

subfiles.about: A report from Bucharest confirming Ion Constantinescu's commercial ties with Japan and explaining his 1944 wartime procurement mission to Switzerland.
subfiles.from: U.S. Mission, Bucharest (signed Burton Y. Berry)
subfiles.summary: Burton Y. Berry transmits information provided by the Chief of the Economic Section of the Romanian Foreign Office regarding Ion Constantinescu. The Romanian government confirms Constantinescu represented Mitsui interests while residing in Japan between 1936 and 1941 as an honorary Commercial Attaché, and that he departed for Switzerland in July 1944 on an official mission to procure military supplies. The current Romanian government considers his Swiss contracts unauthorized, including a multi-million-franc purchase of 500 military radios, and has restricted his passport validity strictly to compel his return to Romania.
subfiles.title: Airgram A-22 from U.S. Mission Bucharest regarding Ion Constantinescu

subfiles.about: A comprehensive report detailing the Bern Legation's interrogation of Ion Constantinescu and his attorney Dumitru Chisalicescu regarding their wartime activities and relations with Axis powers.
subfiles.summary: Minister Leland Harrison reports on an extensive interview conducted on December 4, 1945, with Ion Constantinescu and his attorney Dr. Dumitru Chisalicescu following their request for transit visas to Romania with medical supplies. Constantinescu categorically denied Axis intelligence work or collaboration, asserting that his Mitsui ties involved only a single thwarted tire shipment after 1939 and emphasizing his efforts to shelter Jews and defy anti-Semitic laws in Bucharest. He explained that his 1944 Swiss procurement orders with Zellweger A.G. and F. Straub & C. Meier remained unfulfilled with funds still on deposit, while Chisalicescu detailed his own failed oil negotiations in Stockholm with Enskilda Bank. Constantinescu claimed that accusations against him were fabricated by Max Edelstein, whom he accused of pro-German grain trading and conspiring with Romanian Minister Richard Franassovici to embezzle Romanian state funds in Bern.
subfiles.title: Airgram A-1276 from Amlegation Bern on Interview with Ion Constantinescu

subfiles.about: A report relaying additional allegations by Ion Constantinescu regarding Max Edelstein's espionage ties, Romanian diplomatic corruption, and Soviet NKVD networks in Switzerland.
subfiles.summary: Minister Harrison forwards supplementary intelligence furnished by Ion Constantinescu during his application for a U.S. transit visa en route to China. Constantinescu claimed that Max Edelstein had returned to Bucharest as an Exchange Telegraph correspondent working with Walter Garrett in Zurich, carrying courier credentials issued by Romanian Consul General Georges T. Gallin. According to Constantinescu, Gallin was a former German spy operating as the chief NKVD agent in Bern under Romanian security head Emil Bodnăraș, while Police Inspector General Tabrea and former ONACO director Alexander Fulof were also tied to illicit Swiss-German trade and Soviet intelligence. Harrison asks the Bucharest Mission to review these allegations and requests distribution to Safehaven and Pangerm authorities.
subfiles.title: Airgram A-553 from Amlegation Bern regarding Constantinescu Allegations

subfiles.about: A diplomatic despatch transmitting Ion Constantinescu's formal petition for the release of 312,800 Swiss francs held in the Yokohama Specie Bank in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The American Legation at Bern transmits a formal request from Ion Constantinescu regarding a credit of 312,800 Swiss francs held in his account with the Yokohama Specie Bank in Tokyo from prewar commercial transactions. The Legation notes that Constantinescu has applied for a U.S. transit visa to relocate to Shanghai and join the Asia Impex Company, having already obtained a Chinese visa and secured acquittal in Swiss courts on Romanian charges. Minister Harrison advises that while the Legation sees no security grounds to oppose the transit visa, releasing his frozen bank deposit in Japan remains doubtful due to unresolved Allied occupation policies governing external assets.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 14671 from Amlegation Bern on Yokohama Specie Bank Deposit

subfiles.about: A letter from Ion Constantinescu to Legation officer Harry Conover explaining the origins of his blocked Tokyo bank account and pleading for U.S. assistance.
subfiles.summary: Ion Constantinescu writes directly to U.S. Foreign Service Officer Harry Conover in Bern, detailing his precarious financial situation after four years of virtual inactivity in Switzerland. He explains that his credit of 312,800 Swiss francs at the Yokohama Specie Bank in Tokyo resulted from a legitimate prewar transaction involving tires resold to Mitsui Bussan Kaisha, which Allied Headquarters now prohibits from being transferred abroad. Constantinescu affirms his pro-Allied sympathies, denial of Axis ties, and permanent Swiss residence, urging the Legation to intercede with SCAP in Tokyo so the funds can be remitted to the Banque Populaire Suisse to support his family.
subfiles.title: Letter from Ion Constantinescu to Harry Conover regarding Tokyo Funds
subfiles.to: Harry Conover, United States Legation, Bern

subfiles.about: A State Department instruction rejecting Ion Constantinescu's request to unfreeze funds in the Yokohama Specie Bank in Tokyo due to occupation regulations.
subfiles.from: Department of State (drafted by J. K. MacLennan)
subfiles.summary: The Department of State replies to Legation Bern's despatch No. 14671 regarding Ion Constantinescu's request to release 312,800 Swiss francs held in Tokyo. The Department instructs the mission that Allied occupation regulations strictly prohibit the transfer of foreign exchange assets from Japan, with no relaxation of controls foreseeable in the near future. It emphasizes that broader policy determinations regarding Japanese external assets and foreign claims must be resolved before individual remittances can be permitted.
subfiles.title: State Department Instruction No. 3775 to American Mission Bern
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge of the American Mission, Bern

subfiles.about: A State Department telegram alerting the American Legation in Bangkok to the wartime propaganda work of Siamese national Yoa Suthinun in Japan.
subfiles.from: Department of State (signed James F. Byrnes)
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State James F. Byrnes transmits an intelligence alert to the American Legation in Bangkok based on findings from George Atcheson Jr. and the Counter-Intelligence Section in Tokyo. The telegram states that Yoa Suthinun, a Siamese national, traveled to Japan in March 1944 at the request of the Japanese government to produce wartime propaganda targeting Thailand and was paid by Tokyo until hostilities ended. The legation is instructed to communicate this information to the Siamese authorities for appropriate judicial or administrative action.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram to Amlegation Bangkok regarding Yoa Suthinun
